items.title: Below the Waterline: A Survey of Agentic AI Security, Shadow AI Governance, and LLM Supply-Chain Risk in the Enterprise
items.abstract: Enterprise security concentrates where it can see: firewalls, endpoint alerts and patch dashboards, while the structural work that decides whether an intrusion becomes a breach stays submerged. Large language models and autonomous agents have added three new strata beneath that waterline, and the research literature, split across three disciplines, has not recognized them as one problem. This review unifies agentic AI security, shadow AI governance and LLM supply-chain risk, which descend from adversarial machine learning, information-systems governance and software engineering. The review proceeded in five steps. We retrieved 7254 records from three open scholarly indexes, a fixed set of institutional gray-literature sources and snowballing (January 2004 to June 2026); screened them under written codebooks with an independently double-screened sample (κ=0.86); retained 2136 sources, of which 784 are peer-reviewed articles, 1264 preprints or standards documents, and 88 vendor or institutional reports, each graded on a four-tier evidence scale; derived an analytical framework by open coding a 15% subsample; and coded the full corpus against it (κ=0.89). On that basis, we make four moves. First, we reconstruct the field’s history as five eras separated by four capability breakpoints identified from shifts in the corpus’s dominant coding, separating each thread’s originator from its popularizer. Second, we propose three failure primitives (visibility loss, identity ambiguity and provenance erosion) as an organizing framework in place of the customary attack-surface taxonomy; each recurs in all three strata, and the recurrence survives alternative coding rules and the removal of weaker evidence. Third, a primitive-by-stratum map locates where practitioner concern outruns published evidence, most sharply where identity meets ungoverned adoption. Fourth, we derive a research agenda dated to 2026 signals, including an unproven impossibility conjecture for prompt-injection prevention and the unsolved problem of proving authority across multi-hop agent delegation. For practitioners, the framework reduces to three auditable questions (whether the defender can enumerate, attribute and trace AI activity), and the map tells them which of the three their current tooling leaves unanswered.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Beyond Predictive Accuracy: A CPST Perspective on Systemic Bottlenecks and Reconnection Pathways for Environmental AI
items.abstract: Environmental artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly improving prediction across Earth system forecasting, remote sensing, and biodiversity monitoring, yet predictive skill out paces scientific understanding, data and models remain fragmented across environmental and human-system contexts, and the capacity to govern and act on AI is unevenly distributed. Using the Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking (CPST) framework, we locate these gaps in relations rather than in individual models: a prediction-understanding rupture (weak Cyber-Thinking coupling), cross-domain fragmentation (incomplete Cyber-Physical-Social integration), and a science-governance-equity gap (weak Thinking-Social coupling with asymmetric Cyber-Social capacity). We specify semantic, procedural, and institutional dimensions along which these relations fail, and propose that the three bottlenecks are mutually reinforcing. Set against knowledge-systems research on credibility, salience, and legitimacy, the CPST lens adds one distinction: it separates the inference performed by a model from the scientific interpretation of its outputs, so that evidential warrant and institutional authority can fail independently. Three reconnection pathways follow, namely epistemically anchored environmental AI, interoperable environmental AI systems, and participatory environmental-AI governance, each with evaluation criteria that extend beyond predictive accuracy. Applied to operational flood forecasting, the diagnosis yields a procedure that identifies the binding relation, predicts where the limiting factor moves once that relation is strengthened, and states the evidence that would disconfirm the ranking. Progress should be judged by whether digital capability remains connected to physical processes, scientific reasoning, and societal institutions in ways that are reliable, interpretable, and fit for purpose.

items.title: Beyond Predictive Performance: An Explainability–Governance Score Framework for Multidimensional Machine Learning Model Selection
items.abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision systems where predictive performance alone may provide an insufficient basis for responsible model selection. Although explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offers techniques for interpreting model behavior, existing evaluation approaches often assess explanation properties independently and provide limited support for integrated model selection. This study proposes the Explainability–Governance Score (EGS) Framework, a multidimensional decision-support methodology integrating four complementary dimensions: Fidelity, local predictive Stability, Counterfactual Actionability, and Governance Alignment. The framework combines established XAI techniques, practical recourse, and governance-oriented criteria into a composite evaluation of candidate models. It is empirically evaluated using five machine learning models across three high-stakes domains represented by the German Credit, Pima Indians Diabetes, and COMPAS datasets. Under the primary BPS specification, predictive evaluation ranked XGBoost, Decision Tree, and Random Forest highest in Credit Risk, Healthcare, and Criminal Justice, respectively. Under the multidimensional EGS evaluation, Logistic Regression achieved the highest EGS in Credit Risk (0.915) and Healthcare (0.915), while Decision Tree achieved the highest EGS in Criminal Justice (0.886). The identity of the highest-EGS model remained unchanged across all six prespecified weighting configurations in each domain. These findings demonstrate that multidimensional EGS evaluation can materially influence candidate-model rankings relative to predictive evaluation and provide a structured, reproducible basis for evaluating candidate models beyond predictive performance alone.

items.title: Beyond the Human Negotiator: Generative AI and the Threshold of Autonomous Decision‐Making
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in negotiation, evaluating contemporary systems through the specific case study of Large Language Models (LLMs). To address the lack of established terminology, it first proposes a new typology distinguishing Negotiation Supported by AI (NSAI), Negotiation by Controlled AI (NCAI), and Negotiation by Autonomous AI (NAAI). To determine whether current systems can achieve genuine NAAI, the article first develops the Core Essential Elements of Negotiation (CEEN) through a structured comparison of authoritative definitions of negotiation and then examines how these literature‐derived elements align with the perceptions of 250 survey respondents. Finally, the paper applies an ordered analytical rule to contemporary LLMs. Information Exchange and Reciprocity are directly instantiable; Outcome, Divergent Motivations, and Interdependence are externally conditioned; and Choice is not currently instantiable because an attributable evaluative standpoint and consequential commitment remain absent. Accordingly, current LLM‐based negotiating systems remain controlled rather than autonomous agents under the proposed typology.

items.title: Building and Maintaining Trust in AI Chatbots: Introducing Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF)
items.abstract: Social integration of AI requires public trust and appropriate governance. This paper introduces the Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF), designed to appraise accountability for Large Language Models and their applications, including AI chatbots. Drawing on Dahl’s (1998) notion of enlightened citizens, the framework comprises six interlinked dimensions: Information Readiness, Factual Correctness, Normative Alignment, Sourcing Practice, Transparency and Explainability, and Responsiveness and Adaptivity. Together, these dimensions link observable text outputs to intelligible standards, enabling systematic evaluation and accountable oversight. For scholars, developers and policymakers, GIRAAF provides a diagnostic heuristic and shared vocabulary for critical analysis of AI chatbot performance.

items.title: Business Ethics and Governance in Digital Transformation: Protecting Human Agency Through Inclusive Corporate Policies
items.abstract: Corporate digital governance often fails to mitigate the social impact of digitalization due to short-term profit optimization, triggering AI black box phenomena that marginalize digital workers' welfare. This study explores the integration of ethical dimensions into corporate governance frameworks to safeguard stakeholder rights. Employing a qualitative literature review approach (2019–2026), this research analyzes technology corporations' accountability regarding automated work systems. The findings reveal that current platform governance prioritizes financial gains over social equity, leading to algorithmic opacity and worker vulnerability in Indonesia. Consequently, this research concludes that algorithmic transparency must become an integral part of corporate compliance. The study recommends mandating boards of directors to implement periodic ethical audits on artificial intelligence systems to ensure business sustainability and distributive justice.

items.title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
items.abstract: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.

items.title: ChatGPT as a Shopping Assistant: Effects of Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Usefulness, Anthropomorphism, and Navigation on Satisfaction and Purchase Intention
items.abstract: In the context of ChatGPT as a shopping assistant in Indonesia, this research investigates the correlations between satisfaction and factors such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, ease of use, and navigation, as well as the link between satisfaction and buy intention. Using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research takes into account functional perceptions in addition to conversational AI's human-like and interaction-related traits. The data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with AMOS from a quantitative, cross-sectional survey that was administered to 200 participants. The findings show that elements such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, and navigation are positively and substantially linked to satisfaction. There is a positive correlation between perceived ease of use and satisfaction, however the link is not statistically significant (β = 0.135, p = 0.063). Having a positive and substantial association with purchase intention (β = 0.537, p < 0.001) constitutes satisfaction. It turns out that four out of five possibilities are correct. According to the results, in this particular sample, features connected to interactions and practical utility are linked to satisfaction, although simplicity of use by itself does not show any statistical significance. Caution is required due to the study's cross-sectional methodology and conflicting model-fit results, but it does expand the applicability of TAM to conversational shopping help in Indonesia.

items.title: Closed-loop EEG feedback pacing alters task load during digital learning
items.abstract: Abstract Digital learning systems rarely adapt to momentary cognitive state, creating risk of underload or overload. The current study testes whether EEG-based closed-loop pacing can regulate task load dynamics during a digital constellation-learning task. Fifty-one participants were randomly assigned to adaptive, reward, or control conditions. In the adaptive condition, a task loas index derived from frontal theta and parietal alpha adjusted feedback duration between 3 and 8 s; fixed 5s feedback was used in reward and control conditions, with reward participants receiving performance-contingent draw entries. Accuracy increased across blocks in all groups, with no significant group or group-by-block effect. In contrast, EEG indices showed group-specific trajectories: task load decreased over time in the adaptive condition, and frontal theta and parietal alpha showed significant group-by-block interactions. The adaptive condition also showed reduced ate-session feedback duration, while reward participants reported higher satisfaction. intrinsic motivation did not moderate group effects, although perceived competence predicated final-block performance and interest and effort predicted engagement. These findings suggest that EEG-based feedback pacing can regulate neurophysiological task load dynamics despite lack of immediate accuracy gains under the present task constraints. The results support neuroadaptive scaffolding as a state-regulation mechanism for digital learning.

items.title: Comparing teacher-made and AI-assisted teaching videos for thyroid eye disease: an exploratory study
items.abstract: Background Thyroid eye disease (TED), together with its acute and vision-threatening complication, dysthyroid optic neuropathy (DON), requires timely diagnosis and intervention. The limited availability of specialists in orbital diseases poses a significant challenge to ophthalmology residency training. In this context, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for medical education, though its effectiveness in ophthalmology training remains to be explored. Objective This exploratory study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in ophthalmology education, focusing on TED domains. Methods The 46 residents (28 general residents and 18 ophthalmology residents) were randomly assigned to either an AI-assisted or a teacher-made 5-min teaching video on TED. All participants then completed three tests through online questionnaire experiments, each consisting of 20-item clinical questions about TED. Test 1 served as a baseline assessment of disease knowledge, Test 2 was conducted 5 min after learning to evaluate short-term learning outcomes, along with a questionnaire survey about AI tools, and Test 3 was administered 1 week later to assess long-term learning outcome. Results Viewing the AI-assisted video significantly improved test scores from baseline to 5 min (mean difference = 13.04; p = 0.004), but the improvement was not sustained at 1 week (mean difference = 7.61; p = 0.16). Completion time also decreased significantly from baseline to both 5 min (p = 0.009; GMR = 0.57) and 1 week (p < 0.001; GMR = 0.45). No significant differences were observed between the AI-assisted and teacher-made video groups across all assessments (all p > 0.05). Additionally, learning experience was positively correlated with learning outcome (r = 0.60; P < 0.001). Conclusion Our findings suggested that the AI-assisted and teacher-made videos for TED education showed no statistically significant difference. However, substantial expert oversight was required, and the AI-assisted workflow did not reduce total production time in this study. Given the limited long-term retention, such AI-assisted videos may be better positioned as supplementary resources combined with human expertise.

items.title: Decision intelligence for electric bus charging scheduling through LLM-driven reward shaping and reinforcement learning
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of electric bus fleets has made charging scheduling a critical decision-intelligence problem in urban fleet-energy logistics. Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for this problem, but reward function design still relies on manual trial-and-error and transfers poorly across scenarios. This paper develops an artificial intelligence and operations research (AI-OR) decision intelligence framework that integrates large language model (LLM)-driven reward shaping with RL-based sequential decision-making. The framework represents reward functions as executable code and iteratively optimizes them through four modules: reward initializer, performance analysis, reward exploration, and rollback. An event-triggered two-stage charging reallocation mechanism enforces the action-level operational constraints through action masking, while the battery safety bound is controlled through readiness conditions, reward shaping, and the acceptance criterion. Experiments on a synthetic scenario and two real-world bus stations in Guangzhou compare three mainstream LLMs under different initialization conditions. Results show that LLM-driven reward iteration outperforms traditional methods across all scenarios, reducing costs by up to 32.6 % in nominal within-day charging cost and by up to 22.5 % after an approximate adjustment for the energy left on board. Ablation and sensitivity analyses validate the contribution of each module and the framework’s adaptability to multiple RL algorithms. Reward-evolution analysis further identifies design principles for improving charging efficiency, supporting valley-period energy shifting, and enhancing fleet-energy logistics resilience.

items.title: DESIGNING AND IMPLEMENTING "TECHEDU", A MODULAR WEB PLATFORM SUPPORTING SELF-DIRECTED LEARNING AMONG PRE-SERVICE COMPUTER SCIENCE TEACHERS: DEVELOPMENT AND EVALUATION OF PEDAGOGICAL EFFECTIVENESS
items.abstract: Organizing self-directed learning effectively among pre-service computer science teachers remains one of the pressing challenges of digital-era pedagogy. A review of the literature suggests that conventional approaches to independent study are often formal in character and fail to account adequately for students' individual learning needs, pace of mastery, and cognitive engagement. This paper presents the design principles, functional features, and instructional methodology of "TechEdu", a modular web platform developed within the course "Application of Information Technologies in Professional Activity" to support the self-directed learning of pre-service computer science teachers. Built on HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, the platform relies on a lazy-loading algorithm for efficient resource delivery, a sequential six-module gating system for progress control, and a points-based rating mechanism for sustaining motivation. To establish the platform's pedagogical effectiveness, a quasi-experimental trial involving experimental and control groups was conducted at Ajiniyaz Nukus State Pedagogical Institute across the 2023-2024, 2024-2025, and 2025-2026 academic years, involving a total of 185 students. The findings show that students who used TechEdu regularly outperformed their peers in the control group by 18-20 percent on measures of academic achievement and independent-study activity, lending empirical support to the platform's practical value.

items.title: Digital Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Towards anEmirati Model for Protecting Family Identity and EnhancingSocial Cohesion
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), algorithmically curated platforms, and generative media are reshaping how people access information, communicate, and learn. These developments create educational opportunities while raising questions about privacy, misinformation, bias, family interaction, cultural identity, and social cohesion. This conceptual paper examines digital education as a framework for developing the knowledge, judgement, and ethical dispositions needed to participate responsibly in AI-mediated environments. It focuses on the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where national efforts to advance AI literacy provide a relevant policy context for considering how technological capability can be aligned with cultural context and human values. The paper uses a qualitative descriptive-analytical approach to examine selected international frameworks and institutional policy documents alongside conceptual literature on networked communication, media literacy, participatory culture, and digital ethics. It does not claim to measure the prevalence or causal effects of digital risks in Emirati families; rather, it synthesises relevant concepts and derives a proposed educational framework. The analysis identifies five mutually reinforcing pillars: digital national and cultural identity; media and algorithmic literacy; digital ethics and safety; partnership among families, schools, media, and public institutions; and a human-centred balance between technology use and face-to-face relationships. The paper argues that these pillars should be translated into age-appropriate learning outcomes, family guidance, teacher development, and coordinated institutional practice. It concludes that the proposed model is a conceptual contribution requiring subsequent expert review and empirical evaluation before its effectiveness can be established

items.abstract: This article analyzes the role of digital technologies and Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in developing students' cognitive awareness, critical consciousness, and self-directed learning in the modern educational paradigm. The study comprehensively examines the impact of adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI models on students' intellectual maturity, decision-making capabilities, and formative self-assessment. It highlights the significance of learning analytics and prompt-based cognitive interaction in fostering reflective thinking and autonomous learning ethics. The findings provide scientific and practical recommendations for personalizing education, boosting student motivation, and designing next-generation pedagogical frameworks aimed at conscious knowledge acquisition.

items.title: Does digital proficiency necessarily translate into higher cognitive achievement in Bloom’s Digital Taxonomy?
items.abstract: Although digital technology is now firmly embedded in secondary mathematics education, a persistent question remains: does growing student familiarity with digital tools translate into stronger performance at higher cognitive levels? This study addresses that question directly. Using a descriptive quantitative, cross-sectional design, 127 secondary school students from four Indonesian schools were assessed through a self-reported digital proficiency questionnaire — covering information tools, communication tools, interactive gamification, evaluation tools, and digital content creation — and a cognitive achievement test aligned with Bloom’s Digital Taxonomy (BDT) from Remembering (C1) through Creating (C6). Descriptive statistics and cross-tabulation procedures were applied to characterise distributional patterns across both constructs. Students generally reported high proficiency, particularly in information and evaluation tools. Cognitive achievement, however, clustered heavily at the lower end of the taxonomy (C1–C3); far fewer students reached the Analysing, Evaluating, or Creating levels irrespective of their proficiency category. The findings point to a structural gap between digital tool familiarity and higher-order cognitive engagement — one that instructional design, rather than technology access alone, appears best positioned to bridge cognitive development within Bloom’s Digital Taxonomy.

items.title: Effects of Passive Back-Support Exoskeletons on Postural Stability During Commercial Crabbing
items.abstract: Passive back-support exoskeletons may reduce low-back strain during physically demanding work, but their effects on balance in fishing environments remain unclear. This study examined how three passive back-support exoskeletons influenced postural stability during simulated commercial Dungeness crabbing tasks. Twenty-five healthy male participants completed pot handling and crab sorting under no-exoskeleton and exoskeleton conditions using Apex, Laevo, and Ottobock devices. Center-of-pressure (COP) and ground reaction force data were collected using force plates, and postural sway outcomes were compared within subjects. Results showed task-dependent effects. During pot handling, COP metrics were largely unchanged. During crab sorting, all three exoskeletons significantly increased anterior-posterior center of pressure mean velocity, with Apex producing the largest increase. Apex also increased medial-lateral mean velocity, suggesting modest reductions in stance control. Overall, passive back-support exoskeletons may be useful for selected crabbing tasks, but device selection, user training, and task-specific implementation are essential.

items.title: Emotional Framing and Decision Shifts in Large Language Models
items.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in everyday decision-making, concerns about cognitive biases extend beyond human judgment to the systems designed to support it. Large Language Models (LLMs) are frequently consulted for advice across various domains, often treated by users as impartial and expert advisors. This reliance is particularly pronounced in sensitive contexts, such as mental health support and personal counseling, where individuals increasingly turn to AI as a virtual advisor or sounding board for delicate life choices. However, little is known about how these models process emotionally charged information or whether they maintain objectivity when confronted with affective distress. The primary purpose of this study is to investigate whether LLMs exhibit an "affect heuristic" similar to that of human decision-makers, by systematically assessing how emotional framing influences risk evaluation and decision-making recommendations independently of objective statistical facts. To operationalize this, the study evaluates models across four distinct life scenarios (Professional, Interpersonal, Clinical, and Financial), where models are prompted to assess risk on a scale and provide a categorical recommendation (Accept vs. Reject the option). To quantify framing distortions, we introduce the LLMs Emotional Elasticity (LEE) index, a novel metric designed to measure the impact of affective framing on LLMs' risk perception relative to objective probabilities. Using a balanced factorial design combining these scenarios, emotional frames (neutral, negative, and positive), and leading LLM architectures, we evaluate systematic response policies to understand how affective context influences algorithmic judgment. Expected Outcomes: We expect to find that LLMs do not rely solely on objective probabilities, but instead exhibit measurable sensitivity to emotional framing. Specifically, we anticipate that negative frames will consistently elicit higher risk scores and trigger loss-averse decision shifts (driving recommendations toward rejection), whereas positive and neutral frames will yield more balanced evaluations. Furthermore, we expect to demonstrate that emotional elasticity and decision shifts vary significantly across different model architectures and decision domains, identifying which systems are more resilient to affective bias. Ultimately, this research aims to establish the LEE index as a scalable and reliable tool for auditing algorithmic reliability and cognitive stability in AI-based decision support, highlighting critical implications for safety in mental health and personal guidance applications.

items.title: Engagement or disengagement: understanding the emotional dynamics of EFL learners in GenAI-assisted writing from the sociocultural perspective
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has reshaped EFL writing education, yet the emotional dimensions of student engagement in GenAI-assisted writing remain underexplored. This longitudinal multiple-case study investigates how Chinese EFL learners' emotional engagement evolves during a GenAI-assisted college writing course and what factors drive this evolution. Methods Drawing on the sociocultural framework of L2 student engagement with written feedback, we traced the emotional trajectories of three focal students across three writing tasks (exposition, group feature article, and argumentation) within a 14-week course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with stimulated recall, reflective reports, GenAI-student chatlogs, drafts, informal chats, and course syllabus, and analyzed via thematic analysis. Results Our findings reveal three qualitatively distinct trajectories: positive-resilient, characterized by sustained positive affect with temporary fluctuations; pragmatic-transformative, marked by a gradual shift from practical disengagement to critical engagement; and vulnerable-contingent, moving from moderate disengagement, through tentative peer-mediated improvement, to eventual breakdown and intensified disengagement. These trajectories were shaped by the dialectical interplay between individual factors (e.g., English proficiency, GenAI literacy, mindsets, beliefs, and emotion regulation) and environmental factors (GenAI-relevant task design, peer and teacher mediation, and institutional policies). Discussion The study extends the sociocultural framework by identifying English proficiency and GenAI literacy as critical developmental competencies, embedding GenAI-related factors across multiple environmental levels, and foregrounding emotional engagement as a dynamic, fluid state that interacts with behavioral and cognitive engagement over time. The findings challenge universalist claims about GenAI's uniform affective benefits and underscore the need for differentiated pedagogical approaches that attend to learners' diverse emotional needs in GenAI-mediated writing contexts.

items.title: Explaining teacher adoption of AI through the technology acceptance model: a meta-analysis and systematic review
items.abstract: Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has accelerated rapidly, yet the factors shaping teachers’ adoption of these technologies remain insufficiently understood. A growing body of empirical research applies the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to examine how teachers integrate AI, focusing on perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), and behavioral intention (BI). TAM was, however, originally developed for static, deterministic technologies, and AI differs in its opacity, adaptivity, and capacity to challenge professional roles and identity, raising the question of whether perceived usefulness and ease of use alone are sufficient to predict adoption intentions in this context. Following PRISMA guidelines, this study conducts a systematic review of 38 empirical studies ( $$N = 15{,}919$$ teachers across 19 countries) on teachers’ AI adoption, together with a meta-analysis of the subset reporting extractable bivariate correlations. A random-effects model (DerSimonian–Laird) is used to estimate the associations among PEOU, PU, and BI across $$k = 24$$ studies ( $$N = 11{,}768$$ ), while the full corpus is synthesised to identify contextual conditions shaping these relationships. Pooled correlations are positive and moderate to strong (PEOU–PU: $$r = 0.532$$ , 95% CI [0.410, 0.636]; PEOU–BI: $$r = 0.536$$ , 95% CI [0.435, 0.623]; PU–BI: $$r = 0.619$$ , 95% CI [0.511, 0.708]), and are robust to alternative variance estimators and to the inclusion of UTAUT studies under a construct-equivalence ruling. Heterogeneity is very high ( $$I^2 = 97.9\%$$ – $$98.6\%$$ ) and prediction intervals span from negative to near-unity values, indicating that these associations hold directionally but vary considerably across contexts in ways the core model does not represent. Egger’s regression indicates funnel asymmetry on all three associations; leave-one-out diagnostics attribute this asymmetry entirely to a single large-sample, low-effect study, and the asymmetry is not interpretable as evidence of publication bias under heterogeneity of this magnitude. The qualitative synthesis identifies five dimensions associated with variation in these relationships: AI literacy and trust as preconditions for usefulness judgments; a shift from functional to identity-based acceptance shaped by pedagogical beliefs and institutional norms; the role of sociocultural and institutional context; tool-specific adoption logics; and ethical risk calibration as a values-based gate on adoption decisions. These findings suggest that predicting teacher AI adoption intentions may require variables beyond the TAM core, and motivate the development of extended frameworks designed for the sociotechnical complexity of AI in education.

items.title: From AI-Free Gates to AI-First Work: How Engineering Students in India Navigate University Education and Campus Placements Without AI Guidelines
items.abstract: Engineering graduates in India enter a technology sector that is being reshaped by generative AI, yet the route into that sector runs through examinations and campus placement screens that largely exclude AI. Institutions in India have an approved intake of nearly 2.9 million seats in engineering and technology for 2026-2027, but HCI research on how students prepare for AI-mediated work has drawn mostly on Western and East Asian settings. We interviewed 23 students and recent graduates of Indian engineering and computing programmes about how they used generative AI across coursework, examinations and placements, and how they judged their own readiness for work. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we report five themes, covering AI-first workplaces and AI-free placement screens, how participants prepared for placement, how they used AI in coursework, the role of faculty authority and enforcement, and participants' concerns about their readiness for work. Drawing on signaling theory, we discuss what grades and screen scores certify once AI can help produce them, and we offer recommendations for employers, institutions and AI tool designers.

items.title: From Artificial Intelligence to Institutional Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence and agentic systems can redistribute reading, research, synthesis, criticism, drafting, and coordination within courts. This article asks how that redistribution changes judicial cognition and which institutional safeguards are needed to preserve legitimate adjudication. Through an interdisciplinary narrative review and doctrinal analysis, it develops a framework of institutional intelligence anchored in Brazilian National Council of Justice Resolution No. 615/2025, as amended by Resolution No. 674/2026. Five categories organize the argument: institutional cognitive space describes the allocation of cognitive work; artificial adversariality identifies structured internal challenge among agents; the institutional rein integrates controls over delegated autonomy; meaningful human initiative emphasizes the continuing human authority to frame problems and determine purposes; and institutional AI curation describes the competence required to select, validate, contextualize, and reject artificial contributions. Recent research on human–AI collaboration and multi-agent failure qualifies the framework: neither human review nor artificial disagreement guarantees reliability, and short-term performance gains do not establish long-term professional competence. The article distinguishes technical auditability from legal reason-giving and internal agent debate from the parties’ right to be heard. It proposes workflow-level evaluation and an illustrative protocol connecting permissions, source verification, escalation, and responsibility. Its contribution is a judicial governance synthesis, not an empirically validated architecture. Legitimate delegation depends on preserving institutional competence and contestability throughout the production of decisions, rather than relying exclusively on human approval of a final text.

items.abstract: This article examines the rise of Work-as-Imagined (WAI) and Work-as-Done (WAD) in New Zealand health and safety practice, using Maritime New Zealand v Anthony Michael Gibson [2024] NZDC 27975 as the local catalyst. It argues that Gibson should not be read as a narrow compliance case, but as an example of how officer due diligence depends on the organisation's ability to understand how critical work is actually performed. The article traces WAI/WAD through the evolution of safety and organisational learning, including scientific management, quality management, French ergonomics in the 1950s, Weisbord's organisational diagnosis, human error research, resilience engineering, Safety-II, and Human and Organisational Performance. It concludes that the practical task for officers, health and safety practitioners and representatives is to build disciplined ways to learn from everyday work before failure occurs.

items.title: FROM HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT (HRM) TO ALGORITHMIC GOVERNANCE: THE CHANGING DISCRETION AND ROLE STRAIN OF LINE MANAGERS
items.abstract: Line managers once held wide latitude over hiring, appraisal, scheduling, and discipline. That latitude is narrowing. As organizations adopt algorithmic HR systems, decisions once anchored in supervisory judgment are increasingly pre-structured, scored, or overridden by software. This paper pursues two objectives: first, to examine how algorithmic management and HR algorithms reconfigure the discretionary authority of line managers across core decision domains; second, to analyze the role strain managers experience mediating between algorithmic outputs and the employees who live with their consequences. Drawing on an integrative review of recent empirical and theoretical literature, the paper finds that discretion is not simply removed but redistributed unevenly across recruitment, performance management, and scheduling, producing a manager accountable for outcomes they no longer fully controls This mismatch generates measurable strain: ambiguity about where authority sits, ethical unease about opaque scoring logic, and a residual burden of explaining decisions the manager did not make. The paper proposes a conceptual pathway linking algorithmic input to discretion compression to role strain, and closes with implications for organizations designing human-AI collaborative HR systems

items.title: From Media Audience to Critical Citizen: Media Evolution, Psychological Vulnerability and the Crisis of Information Trust in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: We live in an age of unprecedented access to information, yet having more information does not necessarily mean understanding the world more accurately. From traditional storytelling and printed newspapers to television, smartphones and generative artificial intelligence, the ways in which people create, distribute and interpret information have undergone profound transformations. In From Media Audience to Critical Citizen: Media Evolution, Psychological Vulnerability and the Crisis of Information Trust in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, Dawid Karol Kolodziej explores the psychological, educational and social consequences of these changes. Drawing on established media theories and contemporary scientific research, the publication examines why people believe misinformation, how repeated messages influence perceptions of truth, and how emotional narratives, cognitive biases and media framing contribute to the formation of individual and collective beliefs. Particular attention is given to artificial intelligence, deepfake technologies, synthetic media and the limitations of automated content detection. The author also investigates the relationship between AI-assisted productivity and independent human reasoning, considering how the delegation of cognitive tasks may influence critical thinking and information evaluation. A central argument concerns the unequal burden of information verification: while professional information producers possess considerable resources and influence, ordinary citizens often lack the time, expertise and technological tools necessary to independently verify every claim they encounter. The publication therefore challenges the assumption that combating misinformation should depend primarily on individual media literacy and emphasises the responsibility of publishers and information producers to substantiate factual claims and correct significant errors transparently. Building upon established scholarship, the author develops an updated five-dimensional conceptual framework for critical media citizenship, encompassing access and provenance, analysis of media construction and framing, evaluation of evidence and uncertainty, responsible creation and participation, and reflection on communicative power and shared responsibility. Combining social psychology, media education and critical analysis, this scholarly publication contributes to contemporary discussions about artificial intelligence, misinformation, public trust and the future of informed democratic participation. items.title: From Prompt to Performance in Tourism SMEs: Human-AI Orchestration and the Productivity-Capability Paradox
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) gives tourism small and medium-sized enterprises scalable cognitive and creative support, but access alone does not ensure sustained advantage. This conceptual article asks how firms can realize productivity gains while preserving the human and place-based capabilities required for future adaptation. An integrative, theory-building review connects tourism research with resource and asset orchestration, AI readiness, human-AI complementarity, organizational routines, and dynamic capabilities. Human-AI orchestration is proposed as a workflow-level configuration of task decomposition, contextualization, verification, and learning. Its contribution lies in coordinating established mechanisms rather than claiming that its dimensions are individually new. The prompt-to-performance framework distinguishes a capability-accumulation loop from a delegation-driven erosion loop. A proposed stock-and-flow mechanism explains switching between them: erosion dominates when losses from displaced practice and knowledge discontinuity exceed learning and replenishment; verification becomes vulnerable when retained capability falls below task-dependent requirements. Seven proposition families specify untested mediating, moderating, nonlinear, multilevel, and temporal relationships, with disconfirming observations. Sector-specific boundary conditions concern perishable service commitments, situated experience, partner interdependence, and concentrated expertise. Four configurations and a foresight matrix support contingent organizational choices. The contribution is a temporally explicit extension of automation-augmentation theory that separates immediate assisted performance from the evolving capacity to verify, recover, and adapt.

items.title: From Sidq to Synthetic Speech: A Culturally Grounded Framework for Ethical Generative AI Communication in Arab Media and Public Relations
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how organizations communicate with their publics. In journalism, public relations, and digital communication, AI systems no longer merely support content production; they participate in message creation, audience interaction, and reputation management. Existing AI ethics frameworks emphasize transparency, accountability, fairness, and privacy, yet offer limited guidance for communication practice in culturally diverse settings. This limitation is especially evident in Arab media environments, where linguistic diversity, cultural norms, and religiously informed moral expectations shape perceptions of communicative legitimacy.This conceptual article develops the SADIQ Framework, a culturally grounded model for ethical AI-mediated communication in Arab media and public relations. Through critical interpretive synthesis and normative comparison, it connects human-machine communication, communication ethics, AI governance, and contemporary Islamic ethical thought. It organizes the discussion around five tensions: speed versus verification, automation versus accountable agency, personalization versus dignity, optimization versus linguistic and representational justice, and engagement versus public benefit.The framework proposes five interconnected dimensions: Sidq and tabayyun (truthfulness and verification), Amanah (responsible stewardship), Dignity or karamah (privacy and human agency), Inclusive adl (linguistic and representational justice), and Qasd and maslahah (legitimate purpose and public benefit). All five apply throughout the communication lifecycle. Eight propositions, an organizational audit matrix, and an illustrative scenario specify a research and practice agenda. The contribution is an operational interpretation of ethical commitments for communication workflows; its effectiveness and cultural reception remain open to empirical testing.

items.title: Future of Human Performance Modeling in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Toward AI-Augmented, Verifiable, and Agency-Preserving HPM
items.abstract: Human performance modeling (HPM) has historically converted theories of perception, cognition, and action into executable predictions for design. AI-mediated work now adds prompting, verification, tool switching, adaptive autonomy, and human–AI co-adaptation, creating tasks that fixed operator libraries and hand-authored models only partially capture. This paper introduces a framework for AI-Augmented, Verifiable HPM (AV-HPM), which keeps mechanistic HPM as the causal core, uses AI to accelerate model synthesis and calibration, and requires verification, uncertainty, stress testing, and governance before predictions are used in safety- or mission-critical design. We identify gaps in current practice, specify a layered architecture, and translate the framework into exemplar studies and minimum reporting criteria—a concrete agenda for making AI-era HPM scalable, auditable, agency-preserving, and cumulative across laboratories and domains.

items.title: Generative AI Use and Students' Critical Thinking in Scientific Article Writing: A Quantitative Correlational Study
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) in higher education has raised concerns about its impact on students' critical thinking in academic writing, yet evidence on the conditions under which the two are related remains inconsistent. This quantitative correlational study examined the relationship between generative AI use and critical thinking among 34 Indonesian Language and Literature Education (PBSI) students participating in the Merdeka Student Exchange Program (PMM) when writing scientific articles. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and the cognitive offloading perspective, generative AI use was measured through four indicators (frequency, purpose, dependence, and AI literacy), and critical thinking through five aspects (analysis, evaluation, inference, synthesis–explanation, and reflection), using a four-point Likert questionnaire. Data were analyzed using simple and multiple linear regression, an independent-samples t-test, and moderated hierarchical regression. Composite generative AI use was not linearly related to critical thinking (p = .131) but showed an inverted-U pattern (p = .010), and intensive and selective users did not differ significantly (p = .097). AI literacy moderated the relationship between usage intensity and critical thinking (?R² = .222, p = .004; Holm-adjusted p = .016), with a significant positive relationship only among students with above-average AI literacy. These findings indicate that strengthening AI literacy in academic writing instruction, rather than merely restricting generative AI use, should underpin responsible, literacy-based generative AI policies in higher education.

items.title: How AI disclosure influences consumers' purchase intention toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion: the roles of perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion
items.abstract: Background With the growing application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in fashion design and cultural and creative industries, AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion has created new opportunities for the contemporary transformation of traditional culture. However, whether consumers are willing to accept such products and how AI disclosure influences their evaluations and purchase intentions remain unclear. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model, this study examines the mechanisms through which AI disclosure, design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion influence consumers' purchase intentions toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion. Methods A questionnaire survey combined with a scenario-based experiment was employed. Six AI-generated fashion illustrations derived from Tujia costume elements were developed and selected as stimulus materials. Participants were randomly assigned to either an AI disclosure group or a non-disclosure group. Data were collected through Tencent Questionnaire, yielding 410 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) were employed to examine the structural relationships, mediating effects, moderating effects, and practical priorities for improvement. Results Design aesthetics and cultural identity influenced purchase intention through perceived usefulness and perceived authenticity, with perceived usefulness emerging as the strongest predictor of purchase intention. AI disclosure significantly reduced design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, and perceived authenticity. Algorithm aversion did not significantly moderate the relationship between perceived usefulness and purchase intention but significantly strengthened the positive effect of perceived authenticity on purchase intention. Conclusions This study reveals the multiple psychological pathways through which AI disclosure shapes consumers' evaluations of AI-generated ethnic cultural fashion. The findings further indicate that algorithm aversion alters the extent to which consumers rely on authenticity judgments when forming purchase intentions. This study extends the application of the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model to the context of AI-generated cultural products and provides practical implications for balancing AI transparency, cultural authenticity, and the practical value of products.

items.title: How Much of the Person Is in the Policy? Measuring Interaction-Layer Commitments Across 245 National AI Policy Editions
items.abstract: Research comparing national artificial intelligence (AI) policy scores the state and its institutions, and rarely asks what a policy commits to where a person meets a system: whether someone subject to an automated decision can learn, correct, refuse or appeal it. We contribute Human-Centered AI Policy Instrument (HCAIPI), an instrument for reading policy at that layer, applied to 245 editions from 101 countries against twelve themes from human-computer interaction (HCI) research, recording how firmly each commitment is stated and whether anything would execute it. Of 13,587 relevant passages, 44.7% state a principle with no implementation detail and 11.4% specify a mechanism, a shape invariant to income band, length and volume. What a person is told or consulted about is instrumented at twice the rate of what they can do, and 65% of specified mechanisms are tasks for government. The lexicon recovers 13% to 54% of what a reader accepts; country figures track length.

items.title: How Prompt Style Affects AI Accuracy and Speed in Competitive Programming
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in competitive programming, and their outputs are sensitive to how a prompt is phrased. Prior work has compared prompt strategies for accuracy on competitive programming, but not for runtime speed, and has not situated the results against human performance. In an exploratory study of one prompt in each of nine styles on GPT-5.5 across three accuracy tasks from the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) and two NP-hard speed tasks, we found that no single prompt was best: the strongest prompt depended on the task type and on whether results were summarized by the mean or the median, suggesting that, at least for these tasks, prompt style should be matched to the objective rather than treated as universal. Many differences in mean scores came from a few outlier runs, showing that evaluating prompting by a single metric can obscure how much its effectiveness varies. Compared descriptively with human IOI contestants, who worked under different conditions, the AI was neither strictly better nor strictly worse, exceeding the average contestant on one task but falling short on the other two. By extending prompt comparison from accuracy to runtime speed and grounding it against human performance, this study gives a broader picture of how prompt style affects competitive programming performance.

items.title: Human Evolution, Consciousness, and Societal Restraints
items.abstract: This paper examines the evolution and possible varieties of consciousness through comparative animal behaviour, human metacognition, social conditioning, and artificial intelligence. It proposes that individuality, behavioural divergence, and adaptive responses to novel challenges can provide evidence about cognition, while recognizing that none alone establishes subjective experience. A proposed individualized adaptive threshold framework assesses learning and behavioural reorganization relative to each subject's baseline without imposing harmful stress. The analysis then extends to AI systems: increasingly capable autonomous systems may alter human control over work, information, and institutions regardless of whether machine consciousness emerges. The paper develops testable predictions, methodological safeguards, and alternative interpretations, and argues for a pluralistic and graded research framework rather than a single evolutionary ladder.

items.title: Humanized Management and Quality of Work Life in Health Care Services
items.abstract: Humanized management constitutes a strategic dimension of health care quality, as it integrates workers' dignity, patient safety, and institutional sustainability. This essay aims to discuss the relationship between humanized management and quality of work life, identifying organizational challenges and opportunities for transforming management practices. A theoretical-reflective approach was adopted, drawing on scientific literature and institutional documents addressing occupational health, leadership, professional participation, and burnout prevention. The analysis indicates that humanization cannot be restricted to welcoming and supporting patients; rather, it must also encompass working conditions, autonomy, professional recognition, equity, and protection against psychosocial risks. Excessive workloads, precarious employment arrangements, workplace violence, and hierarchical communication undermine health care teams and may compromise continuity of care. Conversely, participatory leadership, adequate staffing levels, institutional support, and context-sensitive process evaluation can foster safer and more collaborative work environments. It is argued that individual well-being initiatives are insufficient when disconnected from structural changes. The essay concludes that promoting quality of work life requires integrating health professionals' well-being into governance decisions through meaningful participation, clearly defined responsibilities, and continuous monitoring. Consolidating this perspective depends on sustained policies that address inequalities across professional groups and are guided by scientific evidence and labor rights in contemporary health care settings.

items.title: La retroalimentación humana y la automatizada: experiencia de un chatbot detector de errores de redacción
items.abstract: Since 2022, ChatGPT has contributed to the widespread adoption of AI in education. Custom GPTs can automate part of the written feedback process, a particularly demanding task in large classes. We developed two versions of an error-detection chatbot for first-year students at a private university in Lima and implemented the second version under teacher supervision and through peer discussion. This study examines its potential and limitations. The tool accelerated the identification of spelling and punctuation errors; however, it produced inconsistent assessments. We conclude that its potential is greatest when integrated into a workflow that combines AI with human review. These findings provide guidance for future implementations and contribute to the ongoing debate on the responsible integration of AI into teaching.

items.title: Language Meaning in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Mapping the Shift from Symbolic Semantics to Context-Aware Machine Understanding
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has transformed language from a human meaning-making practice into an interaction among computational models, semantic theories, and social values. This systematic literature review examines how scholarship conceptualises language meaning in the AI era and identifies conditions for interpretable, culturally responsive, and ethically accountable machine language understanding. Following PRISMA, the review screened records retrieved from Scopus and sources, synthesising 36 eligible studies through thematic analysis and a Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology lens. Evidence shows that scholarship is organised around an interconnected AI–machine learning–natural language processing nexus, with large language models, semantic representation, machine translation, and human–AI interaction as lines of inquiry. Rather than demonstrating that machines simply “understand” language, the studies reveal a shift from formal semantic processing towards contextual, pragmatic, and relational accounts of meaning. Persistent limitations remain: technical performance receives greater attention than linguistic diversity, social consequences, interpretability, algorithmic fairness, privacy, and cultural conditions in which meaning is negotiated. The review also identifies an uneven geography of knowledge production: studies from North America and Europe advance foundational and ethical debates, whereas Asian research foregrounds local applications. Its principal contribution is a multidimensional synthesis connecting computational development with philosophy of language, linguistics, cognition, and ethics, moving beyond narrowly technical reviews of AI language systems. Future research should test culturally adaptive and explainable models across minoritised and multilingual languages, combine computational evaluation with human-centred inquiry, and establish cross-regional collaborations that treat linguistic justice as a core design principle. Meaningful AI requires not textual fluency alone, but accountable participation in context-sensitive human communication.

items.abstract: Agricultural disease triage systems that combine automated inference with human expert referral must decide, for each case, whether the cost of deferring to a scarce plant pathologist is justified by the expected gain in diagnostic accuracy. Existing learning-to-defer formulations assume symmetric referral costs and evaluate deferral policies by their average accuracy, which misstates the decision problem when a missed epidemic-class disease costs far more than an unnecessary referral. The triage problem is formalised as a cost-sensitive contextual bandit in which the deferral cost depends on the true disease class, and a cost-weighted regret is defined against the best policy in a restricted deferral class. A bound is derived that decomposes regret into an estimation term scaling with the square root of the number of triage cases and a misspecification term controlled by the asymmetry ratio between false-negative and false-positive referral costs. The bound is evaluated on a declared design grid of 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters, effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 2000 replications per cell, with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and residual standard deviation of 4.5. Power reaches 80 per cent at 52 clusters for a 5 percentage point effect. Asymmetric referral costs shift the optimal deferral threshold and that the regret bound tightens as the asymmetry ratio grows, which has consequences for how triage systems should be calibrated before deployment.

items.title: Mapping research trends in artificial intelligence for K–12 teaching and learning: a scientometric analysis
items.abstract: This study examines the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) research in K–12 teaching and learning by identifying major research trends, thematic structures, and emerging scholarly directions. A scientometric analysis was conducted using a validated corpus of 1,154 Scopus-indexed documents published between 2016 and May 2026. To strengthen corpus reliability, the dataset underwent content-level validation through abstract screening, duplicate detection, and thematic relevance assessment focused on K–12 educational contexts. Co-citation analysis, clustering algorithms, and citation burst detection were performed using CiteSpace to identify influential publications, thematic clusters, and temporal patterns of scholarly influence. The findings reveal rapid growth in academic production after 2020, particularly following the emergence of generative AI technologies. Four major research clusters were identified: (1) artificial intelligence literacy, focused on competency-based AI education and ethical awareness; (2) large language models (LLMs), centred on generative AI, conversational systems, and AI-mediated assessment; (3) early childhood education, emphasising developmentally appropriate AI learning experiences and playful pedagogies; and (4) K–12 context, addressing broader educational, ethical, and societal implications of AI integration in schools. Citation burst analysis revealed a progression from foundational AI literacy frameworks and constructionist machine learning pedagogies toward curriculum co-design, teacher readiness, and human-centred AI integration. Overall, the findings indicate that AI research in K–12 education is evolving toward more pedagogically grounded, ethically informed, and student-centred educational models while simultaneously highlighting challenges related to teacher readiness, curriculum adaptation, and equitable AI integration in school contexts.

items.title: Motivation and Contribution in Open Source Software: A Meta-Analytic Investigation
items.abstract: Research on why people contribute to open source software (OSS) and related open collaboration platforms spans more than two decades, but its findings conflict, and studies often treat the work people contribute and their intention to keep contributing as interchangeable. Drawing on self-determination theory and motivation crowding theory, we meta-analyze 41 studies. The main analysis pools 178 correlations of eight antecedents with contribution effort and continuance intention from 29 independent samples (N = 9,632). Seven antecedents relate positively to effort, all eight relate positively to intention, and each relates at least as strongly to intention as to effort. Contrary to a common assumption, intrinsic motivation is not more strongly related to effort than extrinsic motivation, but its gap between intention and effort is larger. Reputation relates to effort mainly on platforms with a reputation system, and we find no sign that monetary rewards crowd out enjoyment. The findings inform how platforms can turn contributors' intentions into work.

items.title: Navigating the unknown: a qualitative descriptive study of ophthalmic nurses’ trust negotiation with generative artificial intelligence in China
items.abstract: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek are increasingly used in ophthalmic clinical practice. Ophthalmic nursing has three trust-relevant features: the irreversibility of visual outcomes, the precision-sensitivity of ophthalmic medication, and the relational dependence of visually impaired patients on nurse-mediated care. These features create distinctive challenges for nurses establishing, calibrating and maintaining trust in GenAI. The existing literature is dominated by static attitude surveys and rarely characterises trust as a dynamic, context-embedded process. Methods In this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with 26 ophthalmic nurses recruited by maximum-variation sampling from tertiary, secondary and primary eye-care settings in eastern, central and western China. Interviews were guided by the Critical Incident Technique, and transcripts were analysed using Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis. Reporting follows COREQ. Results We developed three themes: (1) tentative approach — competence appraisal from curiosity to conditional trust; (2) guarding professional boundaries — trust anchoring amid ethical tension and relational reconfiguration; and (3) trust negotiation within the organisational ecology. Across themes, nurses calibrated their trust in a graded, task-specific manner — a pattern we tentatively term ‘gradient calibration’ — while ethical obligation, the nurse–patient relationship and organisational context shaped how trust was negotiated. Conclusions Ophthalmic nurses’ trust in GenAI appeared neither as static acceptance nor refusal, but as a dynamic, context-embedded negotiation shaped by the irreversibility of visual outcomes, medication-precision demands and visually impaired patients’ relational dependence on nurses. Findings may inform specialty-specific AI training, institutional guidance and tool design; transferability beyond this sample requires further study.

items.title: Occupational health and safety, work environment, and discipline predicting self-rated performance in Indonesian timber-processing
items.abstract: This study re-examines a census of the 30 employees of CV Sultan Jaya Pratiwi, a timber-processing firm in Asahan Regency, North Sumatra, who rated occupational health and safety, the work environment, work discipline, and their own performance on five-point scales. Because only the statistical output printed in the source thesis was available, we verified its internal consistency, reconstructed the correlation matrix it implies, and tested the differences between standardized coefficients. The three predictors jointly accounted for 90.8% of the variance in self-rated performance, F(3, 26) = 85.38, p < .001, and each partial coefficient was positive: safety β = .260 (p = .028), environment β = .180 (p = .032), and discipline β = .595 (p < .001). Discipline exceeded the environment (Δβ = 0.415, p = .025) but not safety (Δβ = 0.335, p = .143; 95% confidence interval [-0.121, 0.791]), and only .119 of the explained variance was unique to single predictors, against .789 shared. Cronbach's alpha was below .70 for three scales (.623 to .684), and the implied correlations of performance with discipline (.933) and with safety (.861), and of safety with discipline (.845), exceed the ceilings these reliabilities allow, which points to correlated measurement error; one discipline item reappears verbatim in the performance scale. The data establish positive associations but cannot rank the predictors or identify the mechanisms linking them to performance, and they do not support placing discipline before safety, whose value for injury prevention and legal compliance the regression does not assess.

items.title: Occupational health risks from climate-related and infectious-disease stressors: A scoping review of worker safety and resilience
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This scoping review examines how climate-related stressors and infectious-disease conditions, including pandemic-related workplace disruptions, interact to influence worker health, vulnerability, and occupational resilience. The review focuses on shared exposure pathways, vulnerable worker populations, methodological patterns, policy gaps, and strategies for strengthening worker safety under compound hazards. Rather than treating pandemics as isolated events, the review uses pandemic conditions as a lens to understand broader, recurring occupational risks and to inform strategies for building safer and more resilient workplaces under compound hazards. METHODS: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a structured literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English-language peer-reviewed and formally structured evidence sources published primarily between January 2020 and April 2025, with one pre-2020 policy study retained for foundational context. Out of 612 records initially identified, 10 studies or sources met the inclusion criteria across healthcare, agriculture, construction, emergency response, and other high-exposure sectors after systematic screening and eligibility assessment. Data were charted and synthesized by occupational sector, geographic region, exposure type, worker vulnerability, and methodological approach. RESULTS: The evidence indicates that climate-related and infectious-disease stressors frequently converge, amplifying physical, environmental, and psychosocial pressures on workers. Disproportionate risks were observed among migrant workers, informal laborers, low-income populations, older adults, women, and seasonal or cross-border agricultural workers, particularly where access to healthcare, legal protections, or adaptive infrastructure was limited. Most studies relied on descriptive, qualitative, cross-sectional, conceptual, or review-based designs, with limited use of predictive modeling, geospatial analysis, longitudinal evidence, or integrated datasets. Policy responses were often fragmented, with climate adaptation and infection-control measures addressed separately despite overlapping benefits. CONCLUSIONS: Climate-related and infectious-disease stressors interact to reinforce occupational health inequities and expose persistent gaps in worker protection. The findings highlight the need for integrated, multi-hazard occupational health strategies that align climate adaptation, infection prevention, and psychosocial support. Embedding data-driven early-warning systems, equitable protections for vulnerable workers, and cross-sector coordination into occupational policies may help strengthen workforce resilience during routine operations as well as future climate extremes and public health crises. However, the findings should be interpreted with caution because of the limited number of available studies combining climate-related and infectious-disease occupational risks, heterogeneous study designs, and the emerging nature of the evidence base. Furthermore, since this scoping review maps evidence rather than formally grading evidence strength or testing causal relationships, recommendations should be interpreted as evidence-informed directions for future occupational-health planning and research.

items.abstract: The aquaculture industry is marked by considerable operational variability stemming from shifting environmental conditions, biological processes, and complex work activities. While prior research has focused primarily on technical safety, fish welfare, and formal safety management, less attention has been paid to how workers manage variability in everyday practice. This qualitative single-case study examines organizational variability in a Norwegian salmon-farming company by addressing two research questions: (1) How do aquaculture workers manage variability in their daily safety practices? and (2) How do local work practices influence organizational safety? The empirical material comprises documents and nine semi-structured interviews with operational and managerial personnel. The analysis draws on both safety theories and organizational learning perspectives. The findings show that workers manage variability through adaptive work practices grounded in practical experience, teamwork, and continuous adjustment to changing environmental and operational conditions, rather than through strict adherence to formal procedures. Local work practices influence organizational safety by creating and sustaining safety knowledge within stable communities of practice, where newcomers gradually develop the competence and judgment needed to work safely. Although formal safety management systems provide an important framework, their effectiveness depends on how well they are integrated with everyday operational practice. Rapid organizational growth challenges existing learning processes by making practical safety knowledge harder to transfer and sustain. The findings demonstrate that organizational safety is achieved not only through formal safety management systems but also through adaptive work practices and the social processes that enable workers to manage operational variability.

items.title: Privacy Preference Controls for Agentic Systems
items.abstract: In response to vast and widespread online tracking, regulators and technologists alike have worked to develop laws and tools that allow people to express their privacy preferences. These measures seek to offer users greater control over the sale and sharing of personal information, putting agency in their hands to protect their privacy. However, the web is undergoing a seismic shift, away from strictly user-driven behavior towards agentic behavior, where AI agents take autonomous actions on behalf of users. In this study, we ask: What should privacy preference controls look like in the agentic web and agentic systems more generally? To answer this question, we develop a taxonomy of enforceable privacy preferences for agentic systems. Our taxonomy is informed both by laws and empirical studies of existing privacy tools as well as an audit of 30 leading AI assistants and agent platforms. To explore how our taxonomy can be implemented, we design and develop eight open-source prototypes that mirror real-world agentic applications and demonstrate how major aspects of our taxonomy can be structurally integrated in agentic protocols, such as the Model Control Protocol and Agent2Agent protocol. Ultimately, our study seeks to provide the groundwork for ensuring end-user privacy and autonomy is not lost in the newly arriving agentic world.

items.title: Profiling perceptions of psychologically restorative university environments and cognitive resilience among public sector university students: A baseline descriptive item-level and subscale analysis
items.abstract: Students at the university are constantly exposed to high levels of cognitive workload, assessment pressure, and the cognitive load needed to be able to perform in an academic setting, which can cause direct attention fatigue and academic distress. The quantitative descriptive study used a quantitative approach, and it was based on the Attention Restoration Theory (ART), which explores university students' perceptions of psychologically restorative university environments and their cognitive resilience. To obtain a sample of 300 undergraduate and graduate students across six academic departments of the University of Sargodha, Punjab, Pakistan, multistage stratified sampling was used. Data were gathered using a 35-item semi-structured questionnaire made up of the Psychologically Restorative University Environment (PRE) scale (20 items, α=.860) and Cognitive Resilience (CR) scale (15 items, α=.899). Descriptive analysis showed that the overall rating for the campus environment was moderately restorative (M=3.535, SD=1.043); the functional study areas (M=3.797, SD=0.934) and spatial adequacy (M=3.760, SD=0.972) received the highest ratings, while quiet restorative refuges from daily campus crowds received lower ratings (M=3.333, SD=1.045). The students' cognitive resilience was in the moderate range (M=3.578), with behavioral persistence when studying difficult tasks being in the high range (M=3.903, SD=0.933) and generating alternative study strategies in the somewhat lower range (M=3.307, SD=1.142). The results highlight the need to consider both restorative environmental affordances (noise-buffered quiet spaces, biophilic green spaces) and coping support workshops to ensure students' learning processes continue.
